steps.body: "How tall is Maria?" has ONE answer. "How tall are the students in your school?" expects MANY different answers — heights vary from person to person. A **statistical question** is one that anticipates **variability**: you expect the answers to differ, and the interesting part is the PATTERN in those differences.

options.label: How many minutes do students at this school spend on homework each night?
options.feedback: Right — different students give different answers, so the question anticipates variability.

options.label: How many minutes did YOU spend on homework last night?
options.feedback: This has ONE answer — your own. No variability is anticipated, so it isn't statistical.

options.label: How many minutes are in an hour?
options.feedback: This has one FIXED answer (60) that never varies. A statistical question expects varied answers.

hints: Which question expects DIFFERENT answers from different people?
explanationVariants: The school-wide question collects many varying answers — that's what makes it statistical.
Statistical questions anticipate variability; single-answer questions don't.
A statistical question anticipates VARIABILITY — many differing answers whose pattern is worth studying.
The defining feature is expected variety in the answers, not the topic or the wording.

options.label: It expects answers that vary
options.feedback: Right — the question is designed around the fact that answers will differ.

options.label: It asks for a number
options.feedback: "How many minutes in an hour" is about numbers but has ONE fixed answer. The key is anticipated VARIABILITY.

options.label: It is difficult to answer
options.feedback: Difficulty isn't the test. A statistical question expects VARIED answers — even an easy one like "how many pets do classmates have?"

hints: It's about the ANSWERS, not the topic.

steps.body: The same topic can produce both kinds. "How old is your teacher?" — one answer, not statistical. "How old are the teachers at this school?" — many answers, statistical. Watch for the switch from ONE case to a GROUP: asking about a group is what invites variability.

widget.prompt: Eleven students answered "How many minutes did you spend on homework last night?" Build their answers: 1 said 10, 3 said 20, 4 said 30, 2 said 40, 1 said 50.
widget.successFeedback: Look at what you just built — the answers SPREAD out. That spread is exactly what makes the question statistical: it anticipates variety. Ask instead "how many minutes are in an hour?" and every dot would stack on 60 in one tower, because that question has only one answer.
widget.partialFeedback: Some stacks are the wrong height. Recount from the data: 1 at 10, 3 at 20, 4 at 30, 2 at 40, 1 at 50.

explanationVariants: Widening from one person to the whole class introduces variability, making it statistical.
The group version anticipates many differing answers — the single-person version doesn't.

widget.prompt: "How far did Ava throw the ball?" isn't statistical. Which rewrite MAKES it statistical?

options.label: How far do the students in gym class throw the ball?
options.feedback: Right — asking about the whole class anticipates varied distances.

options.label: How far did Ava throw the ball, in centimeters?
options.feedback: Changing units doesn't add variability — it's still one throw, one answer.

options.label: Did Ava throw the ball far?
options.feedback: Still one person and one (now vaguer) answer. Widen to a GROUP to invite variability.

hints: Asking about a group instead of one person.
The class version collects many answers.

explanationVariants: "How many sides does a hexagon have?" has one fixed answer (6) — no variability, not statistical.
Even asked of many people, the CORRECT answer never varies — it's a fact question.

widget.prompt: Is "How many sides does a hexagon have?" a statistical question?

options.label: No; every hexagon has six sides
options.feedback: Right — the true answer never varies, so there's no distribution of answers to study.

options.label: Yes; many people could answer it
options.feedback: Asking many people doesn't change the fact that the CORRECT answer is always 6. The data would have no meaningful variability.

options.label: Yes; it uses a geometry fact
options.feedback: Topic doesn't matter; anticipated variability does. A fixed-fact answer has none.

hints: Check each: does it anticipate DIFFERENT answers?
Tomorrow's sunrise time is a single fixed value for one place and day.
Only the bedtimes question surveys a varying group.
explanationVariants: Bedtimes vary across students — statistical. Tomorrow's sunrise (one place, one day) and the number of state capitals are single fixed answers.
Only one option collects a spread of differing answers from a group.

options.label: What time do the students in this school go to bed?
options.feedback: Right — bedtimes differ student to student; the pattern of those differences is the point.

options.label: What time is sunrise tomorrow in our town?
options.feedback: For one place and one day, sunrise is a single fixed value — no variability anticipated.

options.label: How many state capitals does the country have?
options.feedback: A fixed civics fact — the true answer never varies.

takeaways: A statistical question anticipates variability — many differing answers.
Asking about a GROUP (not one case) is what usually invites the variety.
Fixed facts and single-person questions aren't statistical, whatever the topic.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **One answer vs many.** "How tall is your desk?" — one answer, not statistical. "How tall are the desks in school?" — many desks, answers vary, statistical. The group makes the difference.

explanationVariants: The class-wide question anticipates many differing answers — statistical.
One person = one answer = not statistical; a group varies.

options.label: How many books did students in class read this month?
options.feedback: Right — counts differ across students, so variability is anticipated.

options.label: How many books did Leo read this month?
options.feedback: One person, one answer — no anticipated variability.

options.label: How many pages are in this exact book?
options.feedback: A fixed fact about one object — the answer never varies.
